Task 16 writes `terminate`'s body out in full in case Task 5 lands after it; if Task 5 already has it, delete the duplicate rather than keeping two. `ChromiumChild::{kill_only, shutdown}` (`src/browser/chromium_launch.rs:466-500`) are the existing bodies that `terminate` generalises, and their two rules survive it: `wait()` only after a signal that succeeded, and a refused kill is `false`, never a reap.

### 2. What I measured rather than assumed

All on the real `obscura 0.2.2` binary (`obscura-aarch64-macos.tar.gz`, sha256 `607471654d0c…2dfab9`, the same archive the evidence README names), 2026-09-06, against a local `python3 -m http.server` fixture. Commands and raw output are inline in Tasks 16 and 17. The probe scripts are in the session scratchpad (`u3-frametree.mjs`, `u2-boxes.mjs`, `u2b-rects.mjs`, `u-stall.mjs`); they are throwaway and deliberately not proposed for `docs/…/probes/`, but Task 0 should fold their questions into its own harness.

| # | question | answer |
|---|---|---|
| U1 | does `--port 0` work, and is the endpoint announced? | It binds an ephemeral port **and lies about it**: the stdout banner and `/json/version` both echo `ws://127.0.0.1:0/devtools/browser`. Only the listening socket knows the port. Branch ① of the skeleton's two is a URL that cannot connect. |
| — | is the stdout banner a readiness signal? | **No.** It is printed before the bind is attempted: on a taken port you get the banner on stdout, `Error: bind …: Address already in use` on stderr, and exit 1. |
| U2 | what does `getBoxModel` return for a hidden element? | A zero quad, **as a success** — not the constant `[8,8,108,8,108,28,8,28]` fallback the survey warned about. And the same zero quad for the **inline** elements on that page, visible or not. How far that generalises is **U9**, now a T0 probe: the earlier spike's M11 measured five HN elements with real boxes, so my first phrasing ("no inline element has a box") claimed more than one page can support. Corrected throughout Tasks 17 and 18. |
| U3 | does `getDocument{pierce:true}` carry iframe content? | **No.** No `contentDocument`, no `frameId` anywhere; the `<iframe>` arrives as an ordinary element with `childNodeCount: 0`. Always exactly one frame. |
| — | does `Page.getFrameTree` carry a `loaderId`? | Yes for the main frame, and it changes across a navigate. A **child** frame's is derived from its frame id and never changes, so it is not a document identity. |
| — | is the one-shot computed-flags evaluate trustworthy? | Yes. `getComputedStyle` is correct, `querySelectorAll('*')` order matches the `getDocument` walk, and the counts and first/last tags agreed (11/11, HTML/IFRAME). |
| — | what does `getLayoutMetrics` report as content size? | The **viewport** (1280×720 for a 208 px page). No scroll extent can be computed from it. |
| — | does a page busy-loop actually stall CDP? | Yes, and it stalls **everything** on the connection, `Target.getTargets` included — which the survey lists as V8-lock-free. obscura then ends the page's own task at its autonomous budget after ~5 s (`autonomous page task failed: autonomous browser task exceeded its task budget`), `document.title` never reaches `"done"`, and the engine answers again immediately. So a 20 s script does not produce a 20 s stall, and the QA stage is written around a low `cdp_command_timeout_secs` rather than around a number. |

**The asset table is no longer inferred.** The controller verified the repo path and all five names against the real release (`gh release view v0.2.2 -R h4ckf0r0day/obscura --json assets`): 20 assets, five platforms × four flavours, `obscura-{aarch64,x86_64}-{linux,macos}.tar.gz` and `obscura-x86_64-windows.zip` plus their `-stealth` / `-no-render` / `-no-render-stealth` siblings, **no `aarch64-windows` in any flavour**, and `obscura-aarch64-macos.tar.gz` at sha256 `607471654d0c…2dfab9`, 76,038,298 bytes. That matches the table in Task 15 exactly and turns `obscura_asset`'s `None` arm from a guess into a fact. Task 15's "before you start" block is rewritten to say so, and keeps the `gh api` command as a runtime guard rather than as a doubt.

One thing is still unverified and Task 15 still stops on it: whether the release carries a `digest` field per asset. The install path is built on it, absence is treated as a hard refusal rather than a fallback, and if it turns out to be absent the fix is a different checksum source — a design change, not a bug fix. The re-run command is kept precisely because it is the one that shows this.

### 3. Spec ambiguities I resolved, and how

**The capability prose reaches the model as a tool result, not through `DESCRIPTION`** — controller ruling **R2'**, final. (Proposed here, briefly overruled in favour of a literal-plus-substring-guard, then reinstated; Task 16 carries no capability literal and no substring guard. The deciding argument is R9's own: four lines of engine prose on every turn's tool listing is what "prune the prompt" is for.) `AlephTool::DESCRIPTION` is `const … &'static str` (`src/tools/traits.rs:69`) and the catalog entry is `description: &'static str` fed from it (`src/executor/builtin_registry/definitions.rs:72,690`), so runtime injection is impossible either way — the question was only whether to type the generated paragraph in by hand and guard it. It is not typed in. `browser_session{action:"capabilities"}` serves `describe_for_tool()` as prose and `capabilities_json()` as data; the description names the action in one sentence.

What makes that safe rather than merely cheap: a model that never calls the action still meets the gap at the only moment it matters, because `UnsupportedByEngine { engine, verb, supported_by }` names the verb AND the engine that has it. The table is for planning; the error is for the model that did not plan. And Task 18's `caps` stage needs the JSON regardless — a fixture cannot diff against prose.

**`variant = "stealth"` is a runtime flag, not a second archive.** The spec says the ledger installs the `default` (render-carrying) archive and calls stealth "a profile-level opt-in", while the config key is named `variant` — which reads like an archive selector. Resolved: `ObscuraVariant::Stealth` adds the `--stealth` token to the argv and does not change the asset name, with a test asserting exactly that. The config field's doc comment has to say so too, or the key is a lie; that doc comment belongs to Task 6.

**`headless = false` on an obscura profile.** obscura has no window and no `--headless`. Resolved as a `warn!` and a headless launch rather than a refusal: the useful answer is "you got a headless one, switch to chromium for a window", and refusing would make a profile setting that means nothing on this engine into a hard failure.

**obscura's stdio: settled.** The brief asked for stdout PIPED with a drain task, and the `kill` interface change repeated the clause; the controller has confirmed it was carried-over context rather than binding. Stdout and stderr go to `<storage_dir>/serve.log`. There is no endpoint line worth piping (U1: the banner carries the requested port and prints before the bind), so a pipe would buy nothing and cost a drain task; `Stdio::null()` would throw away the one line an operator needs, leaving a `LaunchFailed` that names no door (判据 §14). Recorded as deviation 9, and the module doc states the cost: one log per profile per session, truncated on each launch.

**Port ownership when the probe tool is missing.** The brief said "fail closed if unverifiable". I split that: a probe that **ran and named another pid**, or that ran and found nothing listening, is a hard failure; a probe that **could not run** (`lsof` absent) is an absent instrument and the launch proceeds with a `warn!`. The reasoning is in the module doc and rests on a measurement: TCP bind on loopback is exclusive, and a loser exits non-zero with a named reason, so "the child is alive after `/json/version` answered" is already evidence. Failing hard on a missing `lsof` would make obscura unusable in any minimal container on the strength of a tool we never ran (判据 §18). If you disagree, the change is one arm of `settle_port_ownership` and one test assertion.

### 4. Things I deliberately did not do

- **No `--port 0` branch.** Measured dead; writing it would be a second answer to "where does the endpoint come from" whose only distinguishing property is that it does not work.
- **No `ObscuraChild` type.** Nothing survives between spawn and readiness that `Launched` does not already hold; a `ChromiumChild`-shaped twin would exist only to match a table row.
- **No iframe handling in `fetch_obscura`.** obscura ignores `pierce`, so there is nothing to flatten. The `content_document` branch in `walk` is written anyway rather than `unreachable!()`, so the day obscura populates it the content appears instead of panicking.
- **No capability literal in any `DESCRIPTION`, and no substring guard.** Ruled twice; R2' is final. If a later reader finds either in Task 16, it is a stale edit.
- **No chromium probing in the QA `caps` stage.** It needs a second launch and a second oracle; the stage prints `[UNRUN]` for that row rather than a pass. An unrun claim reported as a pass is the failure mode `qa/README.md` already records for `spend_budget` on Windows.
- **No `[general.browser.obscura] download_host`.** The spec says the existing `[general.browser.runtime] download_host` is reused, same name same meaning. I followed it, and the trade-off is worth stating once: one key now steers two different upstreams (Playwright's CDN and GitHub releases), so a mirror that carries one and not the other breaks the other. The mitigation is that every release error names the host it used.
- **`src/harness/` is not touched by any task here.**

### Addition outside the review (controller, 2026-09-06)

`t0-support-matrix.json` had no consumer — a measurement that cost real machine
time and then bounded nothing. Task 16 gains
`capability_table_agrees_with_the_t0_support_matrix`, which `include_str!`s it
(so a missing matrix is a compile error, not a test that looks nowhere).

**Written against Part 1's shape, per R37**: nested `{engine: {label: {protocol,
effect}}}`, keyed by LABEL rather than by CDP method — three of Task 0's probes
share `DOM.getBoxModel` and two share `Runtime.evaluate`, so a method key would
let the last write win and a capability row could end up derived from a refusal
provoked on purpose. My first draft invented a flat `"<engine>/<method>"` shape
with `{ok, refusal}`; that would have compiled, failed on the first real run,
and been "fixed" by whoever ran it (判据 §10). The rule is one line for both
judges: `Supported ⇔ protocol == "ok" && effect != Some(false)`.

Three of the nine rows turned out to be **not probed by Task 0 at all**, which
I found by reading its probe list rather than assuming: it never calls
`Page.startScreencast` (frames are activity-driven, so a probe that waited for
one would be measuring the fixture) and never calls `Fetch.enable` (arming
interception changes every later request on the connection the other probes
share). I put those two and `multi_connection` in a `NOT_PROBED` list with
their reasons — and R39 then established that none of the three was dispatched
by any verb either, so all three were **cut** rather than exempted. The two
facts pointed the same way, which is what an exemption list is for: "nobody
measured it" and "nobody uses it" are usually one row seen from two sides.
`NOT_PROBED` survives as an empty array so a future genuinely-unprobeable row
has somewhere to go with its reason.

Both effect-judged rows are Task 0's own `reportsSuccessButDoesNothing`
candidates. `drag` is there because obscura answers `Ok({})` and changes
nothing; `js_dialogs` is judged on `Page.javascriptDialogOpening`, whose probe
fires a real `alert()` and waits four seconds, rather than on
`Page.handleJavaScriptDialog`, which on an engine with no dialog records
`{protocol: "not reachable: no dialog event", effect: null}` and says nothing
about the capability. For both, a `null` or absent `effect` fails by name: a
failed read may not be spent as either answer.

### The pattern the reviewer named

Four of the twelve HIGHs were one shape: **a seam chosen so the test could stay synchronous, which then forced the production side to block or detach, after which the test asserted the call and not the effect** — 判据 §4 arriving through the test-design door, in a task that cites 判据 §4 correctly three times. Making `launch_with`'s effects an `async` trait fixed three of them at once (the detached sidecar write, the blocking HTTP poll, and the ordering test that could not see either), and the fourth (`terminate`'s untestable SIGTERM phase) is gone with the function. The lesson is recorded here rather than only in the diff: when a seam's shape is chosen for the test's convenience, check what it forces on the caller before writing the implementation against it.

### Spec ambiguities resolved, and how

1. **`switch_engine`'s approval default — resolved, and then the ambiguity itself went away.** An
   early spec draft said 「默认放行」 with its own next clause saying 「不比 `browser_open` 更危险」,
   and `BrowserOpen` is `Ask` (`src/approval/config.rs:328`). I resolved to `Ask` +
   `inherited_from() -> Some(BrowserOpen)`, honouring the stated *reason* (no second handle-less
   door: an existing `browser_open` policy covers it) without making a browser launch cheaper than a
   tab open. **The spec was then corrected in flight** to say exactly that, so what this part
   records is ruling R6, not a live disagreement. Three places in this file narrated the old draft
   as though it were current; all three now state the fact and name the draft. That is the cost of
   quoting another document by line number — 判据 §1 — and it is why the round entry's ④ no longer
   cites one.
2. **Where `import_state` ends and `switch_engine` begins.** The brief splits them ambiguously
   ("import; re-navigate tabs and restore scroll"). I put *everything on the target* inside
   `import_state` — cookies, tab creation, navigation, localStorage, scroll — and left
   `switch_engine` as pure orchestration (export → launch → import → kill → swap → snapshot). That
   keeps the one ordering claim that matters (`import` before `kill`) visible at a single place.
3. **localStorage ordering.** localStorage is origin-scoped and only reachable from a loaded
   document, so it is necessarily written *after* the first load. Rather than leave the page having
   loaded without it, `import_state` navigates the tab a second time (a fresh navigation, not a
   reload — a reload of a POSTed page prompts). Cost: one extra load per origin that has
   localStorage. Stated in the module doc and, on failure, in a warning.
4. **The "six chokepoints" in SECURITY.md do not exist there.** That enumeration is in
   FEATURE_LOCATOR §3.12 第三轮 A; SECURITY.md has a **four layers** list at `:1864-1889`. I wrote
   the diff against the four-layer preamble and pointed at where the six live, rather than
   inventing a sixth item to match the brief's wording.
5. **TOOL_SYSTEM.md has no browser section and PROCESS_MANAGEMENT.md has no sidecar section.**
   Both are creations, not edits. `rg -ni browser docs/reference/TOOL_SYSTEM.md` returns nothing and
   `docs/reference/PROCESS_MANAGEMENT.md` is 40 lines long, flock plus log rotation.
6. **The ㉑ correction is three things, not one.** The brief named the `channel` key. Reading the
   inventory at HEAD, the second bullet also carries a line-number anchor that has already drifted
   (`chromium_resolve.rs:129` → `:141`), and neither bullet has a settlement. I wrote all three and
   made the settlement say what was deliberately **not** renamed, with the reason, so the next
   round does not re-open it.

### Corrections applied after the review

Four rulings arrived after the rewrite. All four are in the file; two changed a claim the rewrite
had just made, which is worth naming rather than folding in silently.

1. **Only `CATALOG_DESCRIPTION_CEILING_BYTES` moves.** The rewrite had Task 19 raising both
   ceilings. `registry_schema_bytes_ratchet` measures `unconditional_registry_map()`
   (`definitions.rs:3184`) and browser tools are conditionally registered, so that table has no
   `browser_*` row: raising it would account for nothing this task adds **and** break its
   sum-equality guard. Step 6 now says so, follows the protocol at `definitions.rs:1891-1899`, and
   — because Task 16 raises the same scalar first — instructs Task 19 to **re-measure on HEAD**
   rather than add its own delta to a number read from a plan file. Two tasks each adding a
   computed delta to one running scalar is how a ratchet ends up above the thing it measures.
2. **The engine gate is `crate::browser::engine::EngineLaunch { Refuse, Allow }`.** It replaces both
   this part's earlier `EngineLaunchPolicy` (already deleted by the review) and Part 3's
   `LaunchPolicy::may_launch()`. Six call sites updated, plus the consumes table and the two manager
   tests. `prepare_engine` no longer builds a `SessionLaunch` at all — the gate is payload-free, and
   `launch_request_for` already owns that derivation, so a second one here would be its second
   author. The playwright `LaunchPolicy<'a>` now appears nowhere on an engine path, and the
   Interfaces block says so explicitly so it does not creep back.
3. **`set_cookies` takes four arguments.** `import_state` decides the fourth for the whole batch:
   `None` when every cookie carries a domain — which is always true of anything
   `Network.getAllCookies` returned — and the first tab's URL otherwise, for a `MigrationState` that
   did not come from `export_state`. The wire-sequence test now asserts the exported cookie arrives
   **with** its domain and **without** a url, with the rule stated in words (a domain-carrying
   cookie gets no url) because the field's rendered name is Part 1 Task 4's to decide.
4. **Task 20 records the config-gated schema gap.** New item ⑥ in the round entry's
   deliberately-not-done list: the three existing ceilings cover catalog descriptions, the
   unconditional registry map, and the injected/bridge tables, and the 26 `browser_*` tools are in
   none of them because they only exist once a profile is configured — so this branch's new schema
   fields ship on every request for anyone with a browser profile with nothing measuring them. It is
   recorded as a decision someone has to make (what to group by, where the baseline is measured, who
   may raise it), not as a task, because a fourth ceiling added in passing is a number nobody can
   read the predicate off.

Item ⑤ of that same list also changed while it was open: the human-lease hook point is now a doc
comment **inside** `switch_engine`, at the line plan 2 will edit, rather than a sentence living only
in a round entry.
